document.title: Afghanistan: Taliban Official Says Divisions Within Movement Growing; Predicts 'Fight with Iran' (Islama 01403)
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Pakistan: "The Taliban's Godfather"?
document.note: [Confidential] A Taliban official says Pakistan gave ammunition only at the start in 1994 and that the Taliban now capture their own supplies. He adds that Pakistan used Afghan traders to channel money to the Taliban, avoiding a direct link, implying the traders may be conduits for Pakistani government funding.

events.description: US political officer met a Taliban official (apparently Zabul deputy governor) who described divisions within the Taliban
Cable sent from Embassy Islamabad to State Dept reporting Taliban divisions
UN envoy Mestiri met Taliban shura representatives in Kandahar; Omar rejected council proposal
Pakistan allegedly gave Taliban ammunition once at the very beginning of the movement
Taliban captured nine Afghans of Allahudin's tribe infiltrating Herat from Iran with weapons and cash
Embassy political officer met a Taliban deputy governor/participant who described divisions.
Pakistan gave the Taliban ammunition once at the beginning of the movement.
Mestiri met Taliban shura representatives in Kandahar; Omar rejected the UN council proposal.
Taliban captured nine Afghans of Allahudin's tribe infiltrating Herat from Iran with weapons and cash.
Herat shura publicly announced and privately told the Iranian consul that Taliban would respond against Iran.
U.S. Embassy Islamabad cable reporting Taliban divisions.
U.S. Embassy Islamabad cable (SIMONS) reporting a Taliban official's account of divisions among moderates and hardliners.
Taliban shura transferred Ihsanullah to Herat, then appointed him roving inspector general and tax collector after he tried to organize a 3,000-man private army.
Herat governor Yar Mohammed agreed to reopen girls' schools but was overruled by the Kandahar shura.

sources_cited: Taliban official interviewed by US Embassy political officer on 16 Feb 1996
key_claims: Taliban divisions are growing over Omar's ambition to rule Afghanistan and his rejection of the UN interim council plan.
Hardliners allegedly benefit from Pakistani and Afghan trader support while moderates are denied aid.
Pakistan allegedly funds the Taliban via Afghan traders to avoid a direct link.
The Taliban claim to be fortifying the Iranian border and ready for cross-border operations.
The source categorized Taliban leaders as hardliners, swing votes and moderates with tribal affiliations.
Embassy could not confirm that Pakistan backs hardliners, noting no Taliban is very controllable.
